Plates are deceptively hard… honestly one of the hardest forms to make well. This plate demo shows how I use a 3D-printed rib I designed to control side profile, height, and consistency so a full stack actually lines up. Each plate starts with: • 4 lbs of clay • Thrown to about 11.5” for dinner plates-Speckled B mix finishes close to 10” • Rib aligned to the edge of a 14” bat for consistent sizing- still measure with calipers  • About a 3/8” floor for minimal trimming and crack prevention When trimming, I check every foot with calipers and stack the plates in multiple orders to make sure they truly fit… not just once, but every time. Then they dry very slowly under plastic. This part matters more than people think. Here’s a completed apothecary jar and a full overview of how it’s made. For this type of lidded jar, the base and lid are thrown from one continuous piece of clay, then cut open and trimmed to create the inner edges and gallery so the lid doesn’t slide off. There’s lots of nuances when glazing pottery. I think that from an outsider’s perspective it might often look as if you’re just dipping the pot in and taking it out, but in reality, there’s a whole trove of additional thoughts and steps that are being followed in order to get the glaze to adhere to the pot in the way you intend.    If done well, (for me and with the bowls I make), I’m able to coat the vessel in an even layer but I also intentionally catch some excess glaze inside, which I can then swirl around to increase the internal thickness. This does two things, it increases the interest in the glazes surface as the thicker it is, the more the fractal/petal shapes appear, and as this happens on the inside of the pot, there’s no risk that it can melt and flow off of the pot, which is what would probably happen if I applied this extra thickness on the exterior.   That manoeuvre is paired with shaking the vessel to dislodge any pesky globs of glaze from the foot-ring and in the very moment the bowl is drawn out of the glaze, I have to tip out what’s trapped in that foot in such a way that it doesn’t splash and disturb the glazes that’s already adhered to the outer surface…    There’s a lot to think about. If it’s done sloppily and inaccurately, well, then I’ll have to spend more time cleaning up each individual pot, whereas if it’s done accurately, the opposite is true and the faster I’m able to work. Still, with that being said, I still muck up rather a lot. Fluid dynamics, angular forms and a glaze that’s tremendously thick doesn’t make for the easiest glazing process…   #pottery #glazing #glaze #bowl #ceramics
